editorial.headline: Money Changing: Nationally Open, and Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers foreign-banknote exchange and travellers’ cheque purchases; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66125 concerns the exchange counter itself: the buying and selling of foreign banknotes, alongside the purchase of travellers’ cheques. The scope is deliberately transactional. It identifies the two dealings that make up the activity, placing foreign paper currency at its centre and expressly retaining travellers’ cheque purchases within it. For a founder, that matters more than a broad label: the registration is anchored in those stated exchange and purchase transactions. It is a clear definition of what the business is being registered to do.

Registration is open at every stated scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. A founder can therefore place the activity at a micro, small, medium or large business scale; none of the four listed scales is left outside the activity. That range is relevant to its Bali reading, because the record singles out the Besar scale for its OSS risk treatment. Scale does not displace the national ownership result, but it becomes important when the provincial moratorium is applied.

At national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA and foreign ownership may reach 100%. That means a company registering this activity can be entirely foreign-owned under the national entry; the record does not set a lower foreign-ownership cap. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national conclusion is straightforward, but it cannot by itself answer the Bali question, which turns on that province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

Bali’s result is more favourable than a simple reference to the moratorium might suggest. The activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and is expressly not blocked by the moratorium. The stated reason is specific: at Besar scale, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high. Because the province’s rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, that higher risk treatment places this activity outside the moratorium. A foreigner can register it in Bali today, with the national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. This is a direct Bali finding, not an assumption drawn from the national open status.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this activity for PMA: at the Besar scale, its medium-high/high OSS risk places it outside the moratorium.
